# R1 — 1 Thess Opening + Thanksgiving (1781–2317)
**Range read in full:** 1781–2317
**Source:** Weima, 1–2 Thessalonians (BECNT, 2014)
**Slice file:** `.cache/weima-thessalonians-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R1_1th_opening_thanksgiving_1781-2317.txt` (537 slice lines; source pagination/line markers embedded as 1781–2317 content)
**Units covered:** I. Letter Opening (1:1); II. Thanksgiving (1:2–10); Excursus 1 (Is 1 Thess 1:9b–10 pre-Pauline?); Literary Analysis; Exegesis and Exposition; Additional Notes for these units.
**Overflow:** Slice ends with outline stubs for III–V (2:1–5:28) only as navigation headers after the excursus; no body exegesis of chs. 2–5 in this range.

## Claims

### C1 — Letter opening simple because relationship is good
**Locus:** Weima intro to 1:1 (slice § “I. Letter Opening”; ~ll. 1–3 of slice; source discussion of 1:1)
**Quote:** "The letter opening (1:1) has not been formally altered in any noteworthy way vis-à-vis some of Paul’s other letters—a likely reflection of the good relationship that exists between the apostle and the Thessalonian church as well as his overall pleasure at their spiritual condition."
**Claim:** Weima holds that 1 Thess 1:1 is formally unembellished compared with openings that expand sender/apostleship material (e.g., Romans, Galatians), because Paul’s status and relationship with this church are not under dispute and he is pleased with their spiritual condition.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C2 — Three load-bearing points already in the simple opening
**Locus:** Weima intro to 1:1 (~slice ll. 1–3)
**Quote:** "Yet even this relatively simple letter opening serves the important function of laying down at least three significant points that have bearing on the rest of the letter. First, the inclusion of Silvanus and Timothy as cosenders… Second, the identification of the recipients with the term “church” (ἐκκλησία)… Finally, the prepositional phrase “in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” and the greeting “Grace to you and peace” both emphasize the primary and thus crucial role of the Divine…"
**Claim:** For Weima the opening already (1) authorizes the letter via cosenders, (2) identifies the Gentile-majority Thessalonian community with Israel’s covenant “church,” and (3) attributes origin/life/salvation to divine initiative of God and Christ, not to missionaries or converts.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `silas`, `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C3 — Pauline letter opening: three formulas borrowed and Christianized
**Locus:** Literary Analysis of 1:1 (~slice ll. 7–36)
**Quote:** "The letter opening is the most formally consistent section of Paul’s Letters, being made up of three epistolary conventions… sender formula… recipient formula… greeting formula… That these same three formulas… were typically included in the openings of secular letters of Paul’s day… shows that the apostle is obviously not the creator of this epistolary format but borrows from the letter-writing practices of his day. Nevertheless, Paul does not slavishly follow these practices but adapts them… as seen in the way he “Christianizes” the greeting…"
**Claim:** Weima describes the expected Pauline opening (sender + cosenders; recipient as “church” + relationship phrase; “grace and peace” greeting with divine source) as adapted Greco-Roman letter practice, not invented form, with significant Christianization especially in the greeting.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C4 — Absence of “apostle” title in 1:1 is intentional
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a (~slice ll. 50–51)
**Quote:** "The absence of this title here in his letter to the Thessalonians is, therefore, striking. A likely explanation for this omission is that, in contrast to several other letters (esp. Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians), Paul’s apostleship was not an issue with the Thessalonian congregation… Thus Paul mentions his apostleship only once in his two Letters to the Thessalonians (1 Thess. 2:7a), and this single instance serves not to stress his authority but to demonstrate the opposite point… that he… worked with his hands… rather than become a burden to them."
**Claim:** Weima attributes omission of “apostle” in 1 Thess 1:1 (and nearly throughout both letters) to unchallenged status; the one later use (2:7a) is self-sacrificial, not authoritarian self-assertion.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C5 — Cosenders do not mean co-authorship; “we” is literary
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a on cosenders (~slice ll. 52–54)
**Quote:** "Against this scenario, however, are three instances in the letter where the text shifts significantly to the first-person singular… 2:18… 3:1–2 and 3:5… 5:27… These three texts (see also 2 Thess. 2:5 and 3:17) suggest that, though the names of Silvanus and Timothy are included as cosenders, Paul is the real author of the letter, so that the plurals used throughout the correspondence ought to be taken literarily rather than literally."
**Claim:** Weima rejects a “group project” model of composition: first-person singulars (1 Thess 2:18; 3:1–5; 5:27; also 2 Thess 2:5; 3:17) show Paul as real author; plurals are literary.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `silas`, `timothy`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C6 — Why Silvanus and Timothy are named: authority and shared stance
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a (~slice ll. 55–56)
**Quote:** "A more likely reason for including the names of Silvanus and Timothy is that both have played a key role in the Thessalonian congregation: Silvanus in the establishing of the church (Acts 17:1–10), and Timothy in the subsequent strengthening of the church (1 Thess. 3:1–5). The inclusion of these two men as cosenders, therefore, gives further weight or authority to Paul’s letter; it not only shows the Thessalonians that the apostle is well informed about the current situation in their congregation but also that there is agreement between Paul and these other leaders about the response expected from the recipients in their present circumstances (Wanamaker 1990: 68)."
**Claim:** Weima (with Wanamaker) rejects mere courtesy or letter-carrier listing as primary motive; cosenders signal Timothy-informed knowledge of the church and unified leadership expectations.
**Target pages:** `silas`, `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C7 — Silvanus = Silas; senior associate over Timothy
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a biographical notes (~slice ll. 57–60)
**Quote:** "The “Silvanus” mentioned in the letters of Paul and Peter is almost certainly the same person identified as “Silas” in Acts. The longer name was the one commonly known and used in Greek and Roman communities… whereas the shorter name was employed in Jewish circles… That the name of Silvanus is listed before that of Timothy as a cosender of 1 Thessalonians likely reflects the role that each one played in Paul’s ministry. Silvanus took Barnabas’s place as Paul’s senior associate… and Timothy similarly replaced John Mark as Paul’s junior associate…"
**Claim:** Weima identifies Silvanus with Acts’ Silas; listing order marks Silvanus as senior associate (mission-founding at Thessalonica) and Timothy as junior associate.
**Target pages:** `silas`, `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`

### C8 — Timothy’s relationship to Paul and to this letter
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1a (~slice ll. 61–62)
**Quote:** "Timothy, despite his junior associate status, enjoyed an especially close relationship with Paul, evident in the apostle’s reference to him… as “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:17)… Timothy then rejoined Paul, who by this time was in Corinth, and brought to the apostle not only a good report about the Thessalonians’ enduring faith despite persecution and their ongoing love for Paul (3:6) but also news about some areas where they were “lacking” in their faith (3:10). This information from Timothy motivated Paul to write 1 Thessalonians."
**Claim:** Weima presents Timothy as Paul’s close junior coworker, present at founding and sent back to strengthen faith under opposition; Timothy’s Corinth report (good news + lacks) motivates 1 Thessalonians.
**Target pages:** `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C9 — ekklēsia = new people of God continuous with Israel’s designation
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1b (~slice ll. 68–69)
**Quote:** "Although the noun ekklēsia (church) in secular Greek refers to an officially summoned assembly of citizens… in the LXX it… describes the people of God… “it seems unreasonable to doubt that in I Thess. 1,1 Paul is thinking of the Christians of Thessalonica as members of the ‘Church of God,’ and that he is fully aware of the biblical background and theological implications of his use of the term” (Deidun 1981: 11; also Malherbe 2000: 99). That the term ekklēsia reflects Paul’s understanding of the predominantly Gentile church of Thessalonica as the new people of God is confirmed by his reference to them a mere three verses later as those who are “loved by God” and who know their “election” (1:4)…"
**Claim:** Weima (following Deidun/Malherbe) reads ἐκκλησία in 1:1 theologically via LXX Israel language, not primarily as civic assembly; the Gentile-majority Thessalonian church is cast as new people of God—confirmed by 1:4 “loved by God” / “election.”
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C10 — “In God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”: divine initiative; high Christology
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1b (~slice ll. 70–73)
**Quote:** "What ought not to be overlooked in this debate, however, is what both interpretations have in common: the primary and thus crucial role of the Divine, both God and Christ, in the origin and ongoing life of the Thessalonian congregation… That the same pattern is found in Paul’s other letter openings… is similarly important for understanding the apostle’s Christology… “It is easy to forget that here is a Jew who in his younger years would not have dared breathe the name of YHWH but who now as a matter of course puts θεός and Jesus together as the compound object in a single prepositional phrase.” (Fee 2007: 49n62)… That Paul does not feel the need to explain or justify this juxtaposition suggests that the apostle possesses a high Christology, which would have been an important part of his missionary preaching…"
**Claim:** Whether spatial or instrumental, “in God… and the Lord Jesus Christ” centers divine agency; Weima (with Fee) treats the single-preposition compound object as high Christology already assumed by readers, reinforced by repeated God–Jesus coupling in both Thessalonian letters and by the title “Lord” (LXX YHWH / pagan divine title).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C11 — “Grace to you and peace” as Christianized Greco-Jewish hybrid greeting
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:1c (~slice ll. 78–86)
**Quote:** "Therefore neither Hellenistic nor Semitic letters provide an exact parallel to Paul’s opening greeting “Grace to you and peace.”… it is more likely that the apostle takes the typically secular or Greek greeting chairein and “Christianizes” it into the similar-sounding charis (grace… Fee [2009: 17] calls this “a marvelous example of Paul’s ‘turning into gospel’ everything he sets his hand to”). Thus Paul adds charis to the typically Jewish greeting “peace” so that the new combination of “Grace and peace” results in a salutation that is truly inclusive of his Gentile Christian and Jewish Christian audience… Grace is the supreme gift of God’s undeserved favor… “Peace,” or shalom… involves not the Greek sense of the absence of conflict but the Jewish notion of wholeness…"
**Claim:** Weima argues Paul’s greeting lacks exact Greco-Roman or Semitic parallels; best explained as Christianization of χαίρειν → χάρις plus Jewish “peace/shalom” (wholeness, not mere non-conflict), signaling divine grace and restored fellowship.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C12 — Shorter greeting original; longer “from God our Father…” is secondary assimilation
**Locus:** Additional Note on 1:1 (~slice ll. 88–91)
**Quote:** "After the opening greeting “Grace and peace,” several MSS… add the prepositional phrase “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”… Nevertheless, the short reading enjoys textual support from both Alexandrian and Western text types… the longer reading is almost certainly a later addition that attempts to make this brief greeting conform to the lengthier greeting found in Paul’s other letters (so B. Metzger 1994: 561)."
**Claim:** Weima (with Metzger) prefers the shorter 1:1 greeting as original; the expanded divine-source clause is a scribal assimilation to other Pauline openings.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C13 — Thanksgiving’s three persuasive functions
**Locus:** Intro + Literary Analysis “Function” of 1:2–10 (~slice ll. 106–107, 140–150)
**Quote:** "Paul uses the thanksgiving section to accomplish three key goals: (1) to reestablish his relationship with his readers, (2) to implicitly exhort them to live up to the praise that he brings to God for them, and (3) to foreshadow the four major issues that he will address in the rest of the letter… First, this epistolary unit has a “pastoral” function… Second, the thanksgiving has an “exhortative” function… Third, the thanksgiving has an “epistolary” or “foreshadowing” function. In modern movie jargon, it is a “preview of coming attractions” (Witherington 2006: 52)."
**Claim:** Weima synthesizes pastoral reconnection, implicit/explicit parenesis, and thematic foreshadowing as the three standard functions of Pauline thanksgivings; 1 Thess 1:2–10 exemplifies all three.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `paul-apostle`

### C14 — Origin of Pauline thanksgiving: Hellenistic form, Jewish content
**Locus:** Literary Analysis “Source” (~slice ll. 116–122)
**Quote:** "Is Paul’s custom of including a thanksgiving section in his letters a standard practice of ancient letter writing or a new literary convention that he himself developed?… The best answer is probably a synthesis of the two views: the form of the thanksgiving sections is largely Hellenistic, but its content is influenced mainly by Judaism… although to a large extent the Pauline thanksgiving owes its existence and structure to the standard epistolary form in Hellenistic letter writing, its contents are influenced by OT and Jewish thought (so Wiles 1974: 160; Fitzmyer 1968: 225; O’Brien 1977: 11; 1982: 8)."
**Claim:** Weima rejects pure Hellenism or pure Jewish novelty: Greco-Roman letter thanksgivings supply form/existence; OT/Jewish thought shapes content; Pauline thanksgivings differ in spiritual focus, formal length/complexity, and near-universality in his corpus.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C15 — Form analysis: Jervis’s five units preferred over Schubert’s types
**Locus:** Literary Analysis “Form” (~slice ll. 123–140)
**Quote:** "Despite the importance of Schubert’s groundbreaking work… his formal analysis suffers from a couple of weaknesses… An attempt to address both concerns has been undertaken by Jervis (1991: 86–109)… Jervis proposes that there is only one type of Pauline thanksgiving, within which there may occur five distinct units: 1. Principal Verb… 2. Manner of Thanksgiving… 3. Cause of Thanksgiving… 4. Explanation… 5. Prayer Report…"
**Claim:** Weima adopts (with caveats) Jervis’s five-unit functional form over Schubert’s two/three formal types; 1 Thess 1:2–10 has principal verb, manner, cause(s), and explanation, but **lacks** a closing prayer report (present in 2 Thess 1:11–12 and some other letters).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C16 — Extent of thanksgiving is 1:2–10, not Schubert’s 1:2–3:13
**Locus:** Literary Analysis “Extent of the Passage” (~slice ll. 152–187)
**Quote:** "According to Schubert (1939: 17–27), what appears to be three separate thanksgivings (1:2–5; 2:13; 3:9–13) is actually one long thanksgiving… “the thanksgiving itself constitutes the main body of I Thessalonians”… There are serious difficulties, however, with this conclusion… There is overwhelming evidence, therefore, that the thanksgiving section in 1 Thessalonians does not include the whole of 1:2–3:13 but is limited to 1:2–10 (so the majority of commentators…)."
**Claim:** Weima rejects Schubert’s single mega-thanksgiving equaling the letter body: it would be >4× longer than other thanksgivings, redefines function, ignores body conventions (autobiography 2:1–12; apostolic parousia 2:17–3:10; prayer-wishes 3:11–13), and misreads 2:13 / 3:9–10; disclosure formula + “brothers” + tone shift at 2:1 mark body onset; eschatological climax at 1:10 is a sequence-terminator.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C17 — Four major body themes foreshadowed in 1:2–10
**Locus:** Intro + Extent list (~slice ll. 106–107, 159–168)
**Quote:** "…to foreshadow the four major issues that he will address in the rest of the letter (the defense of Paul’s integrity [2:1–20; 3:6–10]; the persecution endured by the Thessalonian believers [3:1–10]; proper moral conduct [4:1–12; 5:12–22]; and the second coming of Christ [4:13–18; 5:1–11])… a. The apologetic reference… 1:5… anticipates… 2:1–16… b. The theme of persecution found in 1:6b… c. The purpose of the Thessalonians’ conversion, “to serve a living and true God” (1:9c), anticipates the exhortations… d. The eschatological subject of Christ’s return… 1:3… 1:10…"
**Claim:** Weima’s structural claim: thanksgiving previews (a) integrity/apology (1:5, 1:9a εἴσοδος → 2:1–16), (b) persecution/imitation (1:6 → 2:13–16; 3:1–5), (c) moral service/holiness (1:9c; possibly idol-cult sexual foreshadow of 4:3–8), (d) parousia/resurrection/wrath (1:3, 1:10 → 4:13–18; 5:1–11; also 2:16 wrath).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C18 — Secondary foreshadowings: election, joy, covenant “loved by God”
**Locus:** Extent list e–g (~slice ll. 170–178)
**Quote:** "e. The divine initiative in the conversion of the Thessalonians is presented in 1:4 (“your election/calling”) as the ultimate cause for giving thanks… reappear[s]… (2:12; 3:3b; 4:7; 5:9, 24). f. The theme of “joy”… 1:6b… 2:19–20 and 3:9. g. …the unparalleled vocative phrase “loved by God” (1:4) may look ahead to the ground of Paul’s argumentation in 4:1–12… covenant language… reapplies it to the predominantly Gentile church… (… see Weima 1996)."
**Claim:** Beyond the four major themes, Weima finds election/calling, Spirit-given joy, and reapplied Israel-covenant love language preparing later body argumentation (including holiness appeals grounded in new-covenant status).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C19 — Structure of 1:2–10: four main clauses
**Locus:** Structure of the Passage (~slice ll. 190–232)
**Quote:** "The thanksgiving section consists of four main clauses: verses 2–5, 6–7, 8, and 9–10 (contra Best 1977: 65, who states that 1:2–10 constitutes “one long untidily constructed sentence”… Fee 2009: 19 sees “two very long and complex sentences: vv. 2–5 and 6–10”). The first main clause (vv. 2–5) is the thanksgiving proper… The final three main clauses (vv. 6–7, 8, 9–10)… function as the “explanatory” unit… Outline… A. The statement of thanksgiving (1:2a) B. The manner… (1:2b) C. The immediate cause… (1:3) D. The ultimate cause… (1:4–5) E. Additional causes… (1:6–10)…"
**Claim:** Weima parses 1:2–10 into four main clauses (not one untidy sentence), mapping Jervis-style elements onto statement, manner, immediate cause (1:3), ultimate cause (1:4–5: election + genuineness of ministry), then additional causes: exemplary life (6–7), evangelism (8), conversion (9–10).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C20 — Thanksgiving directed to God, not human praise, because of election
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:2a (~slice ll. 242–243)
**Quote:** "Even though the Thessalonians are to be praised for their faith, love, and hope (1:3); their exemplary life amid persecution (1:6–7); their evangelistic activity (1:8); and their conversion (1:9–10); and even though Paul and his fellow missionaries are to be praised for the genuineness of their original ministry in Thessalonica (1:5), all of these good things that have happened in the Thessalonian church are ultimately due to God’s work of election (1:4), and so God is the one to whom thanksgiving must be given."
**Claim:** Weima’s theological accent: human fidelity and missionary sincerity are real but secondary; election makes God the sole proper object of thanksgiving.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C21 — “Concerning you all” may deliberately include the problematic
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:2a (~slice ll. 244)
**Quote:** "Some have interpreted this prepositional phrase polemically, so that Paul here give thanks “not only for his faithful supporters, but for the idle, fainthearted, weak (5:14), and the ones who actually oppose him” (Wiles 1974: 180… Fee 2009: 20). Although there is an obvious danger in reading too much into the occurrence of the adjective “all,”… its presence here cannot be easily dismissed as being merely “formulaic”… the deliberate addition of “all” would certainly be in keeping with Paul’s practice elsewhere of adapting the thanksgiving section so that it foreshadows issues addressed later…"
**Claim:** Weima cautiously allows that πάντων may intentionally encompass the whole church including those later rebuked (idle, fainthearted, weak, possible opponents), given rarity in other thanksgivings and foreshadowing habits.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C22 — “Always / constantly” hyperbolic yet credible given family rhetoric
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:2a–b (~slice ll. 246–247, 262)
**Quote:** "But even though these claims are formulaic and somewhat hyperbolic, they may be more credible than first thought when one considers the intimate family language and imagery used in the letter… “brothers”… “a nursing mother”… “a father with his children”… “orphaned”… Here the reference to prayers, along with 3:10… suggests a picture of Paul, Silvanus (Silas), and Timothy meeting daily for prayer and thanking God for the blessings evident in the lives of the converts in Thessalonica."
**Claim:** Weima treats πάντοτε / ἀδιαλείπτως as formulaic hyperbole that is still pastorally credible; manner of thanks is intercessory mention in shared missionary prayer, with gratitude prioritized over petition.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `silas`, `timothy`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C23 — Faith–love–hope triad: emphasis on work, labor, steadfastness
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:3 (~slice ll. 271–278)
**Quote:** "The first or “immediate” reason for giving thanks in 1:3, which focuses on the activity of the Thessalonian believers, can be distinguished from the second or “ultimate” reason in 1:4, which focuses on the activity of God… The direct objects of the missionaries’ act of remembering, however, are the first members of the triad, and so the emphasis is on the Thessalonians’ “work, labor, and steadfastness” rather than their “faith, love, and hope.”… The sense is captured well by the NIV… “your work produced by faith, your labor prompted by love, and your endurance inspired by hope.”"
**Claim:** Weima distinguishes immediate (human activity, 1:3) vs ultimate (divine election, 1:4) causes; grammatically stresses work/labor/steadfastness as products of faith/love/hope (subj. gen. / gen. of source), not a bare generic triad.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C24 — “Work of faith”: not legalism; likely loyalty amid persecution
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:3 (~slice ll. 279–281)
**Quote:** "…although Paul was vehemently opposed to “legalism”… the apostle was by no means antinomian… The phrase “work of faith,” then, refers to the Christian activity that results from faith—what Paul elsewhere refers to as “faith working itself out in acts of love” (Gal. 5:6)… The most likely option, however, is that Paul is thinking of the Thessalonians’ loyalty to Christ (faith = “faithfulness”: Best 1977: 68) amid persecution (1:6; Furnish 2007: 41…)."
**Claim:** Weima reconciles “work” + “faith” with anti-legalist Paul (singular “work” can be positive); prefers reading “work of faith” as faithfulness under affliction, foreshadowing dense later “faith” language (esp. ch. 3), over pure evangelism or generic holy-life readings.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C25 — “Labor of love”: mutual love, possibly against idler exploitation
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:3 (~slice ll. 282–286)
**Quote:** "…“labor of love” refers to the deeds that stem from love… a more likely interpretation is suggested: the apostle is thinking of the subject of love for others foreshadowed in the transitional prayer of 3:12–13… and taken up more fully in 4:9–12… It may well be, therefore, that the phrase “labor of love” has in view the problem of the rebellious idlers who are addressed briefly in this letter (5:14 in addition to 4:11c, 12b) and extensively in the second correspondence (2 Thess. 3:6–15)."
**Claim:** Weima rejects English idiom “labor of love = unpaid hobby”; κόπος is stronger than ἔργον (hardship). Preferred referent: mutual brotherly love (3:12–13; 4:9–12), possibly shadowed by idle freeloaders later treated in 1 Thess 5:14 and 2 Thess 3:6–15.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C26 — “Steadfastness of hope” climactic; hope = imminent parousia deliverance
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:3 (~slice ll. 287–289)
**Quote:** "The third noun phrase, “steadfastness of hope,” stands in the final and thus climactic position in the triad… The word “steadfastness” (ὑπομονή)… is commonly used… in connection with the difficulties and persecution… especially in an eschatological context… the hope… is a confident belief “in our Lord Jesus Christ”… it is clear that Paul is referring… to their very specific hope in Christ’s imminent return from heaven to bring about their deliverance…"
**Claim:** Weima reads ὑπομονὴ τῆς ἐλπίδος as endurance under real opposition, climactic in the triad, specified by “in our Lord Jesus Christ” as hope in imminent return (confirmed by 1:10), not vague optimism.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C27 — “Before our God and Father” modifies hope (third option preferred)
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:3 close (~slice ll. 290–291)
**Quote:** "There are three possibilities as to what this phrase modifies: (1) the participial “remembering”… (2) the three noun phrases… or (3) the third noun phrase, especially the word “hope”… it is more natural to connect the phrase “before our God and Father” with the immediately preceding words, just as in 2:19 and 3:13… the hope of the Thessalonians and of the missionaries… in Christ’s return was a hope they manifested together in the presence of the Father."
**Claim:** Weima prefers option (3): ἔμπροσθεν modifies (esp.) hope, making God witness to shared eschatological hope; rejects tautological reading with “we give thanks to God.”
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C28 — “Brothers loved by God” reapplies Israel-elect language to mixed church
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:4 (~slice ll. 301–307)
**Quote:** "In the two brief letters… the vocative plural “brothers”… occurs twenty-one times—the highest occurrence per number of verses by far… The second cause of thanksgiving is further emphasized by the addition of the remarkable participial phrase “loved by God,” which is not found elsewhere in Paul’s writings… here too we have an instance of language that originally applied to Israel… now being reapplied to the Christian church… “It is clear [from the phrase “loved by God” in 1:4] that by this early stage in his thinking Paul has already developed the concept of the church as the Israel of God.” (Marshall 1990: 262)"
**Claim:** Weima (with Marshall/Thielman; cf. Weima 1996) treats ἀδελφοὶ ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ as Israel-covenant diction transferred without defense to a Gentile-majority church, marking renewed Israel identity; vocative also marks structural stress of the second cause.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C29 — Election as exclusive divine act, rooted in love; comforts and challenges
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:4 (~slice ll. 308–315)
**Quote:** "…it seems quite clear that the apostle believed election to be exclusively an act of God… Still others consider election… offensive… Yet here in 1:4, as in other occasions… election is intimately linked to God’s love. The Thessalonians’ election is not the result of God’s capricious choice but of his great love… First and foremost, it comforts the church… their salvation and final destiny rests not in their own imperfect abilities… but in “the living and true God” (1:9), who has chosen them. Yet the knowledge of their election also implicitly challenges them… to continue to live in a manner appropriate to their calling."
**Claim:** Weima rejects human-choice-first readings of 1:4 and arbitrary-tyrant caricatures; election is God’s exclusive act, love-linked, already part of founding preaching (term used without explanation), functioning pastorally as comfort under persecution and as implicit parenesis; theme recurs via calling/appointing (2:12; 3:3b; 4:7; 5:9, 24).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C30 — 1:5 as apologetic foreshadowing of 2:1–16; ὅτι epexegetical
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:5 (~slice ll. 317–326)
**Quote:** "In all other thanksgivings Paul focuses primarily on his readers… here in 1:5 the apostle also focuses heavily on himself… When these unique features of 1:5 are combined with the fact that the thanksgiving section typically functions to foreshadow the central concerns of the letter as a whole, it becomes clear that Paul in 1 Thessalonians is very much concerned with defending his character and already here in 1:5 anticipates the lengthy defense that he will present at the beginning of the letter body (2:1–16)… Two factors… indicate that the ὅτι here has an epexegetical, or explanatory, function (“namely, that…”)."
**Claim:** Weima reads 1:5 as unique apologetic material inside a thanksgiving: personal “our gospel,” antithesis, three-noun emphasis, and appeal to “you know” prefigure 2:1–16; ὅτι after “know… election” is epexegetical (historical occasion/manner of election), not merely a second proof of election.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C31 — “Not in word alone but also in power—Holy Spirit and much conviction”
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:5a + Additional Note (~slice ll. 327–339, 472)
**Quote:** "This in turn implies that the contrast is only between “word” and “power”… and that the subsequent two nouns (“Holy Spirit” and “much conviction”) are intended to qualify “power”… “Our gospel was not among you in word alone but also in power—both in the Holy Spirit and much conviction.”… Paul’s point is that his gospel message was not only a “heard word” but also an “experienced power.”… “much conviction” is best seen as referring to the boldness and confidence with which the missionaries presented their message… (so most commentators…)—a point that Paul emphasizes again in 2:2…"
**Claim:** Preferring omission of ἐν before πληροφορίᾳ, Weima construes Spirit + conviction as qualifiers of “power,” not a flat triad parallel to λόγος. “Alone” protects preaching’s necessity; power = Spirit-effected reality in hearers (likely including miracles/prophecy) vs flattering “word alone” (cf. 2:5). Conviction primarily missionaries’ boldness, not only converts’ persuasion.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C32 — “As you know… among you because of you”: disclosure appeals
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:5b (~slice ll. 340–341)
**Quote:** "The expression “you know” (οἴδατε)… is the first occurrence of a number of the letter’s direct appeals to the Thessalonians’ recollection… (2:1, 2, 5, 10, 11; 3:3, 4; 4:2; 5:2…)… It is as if Paul is saying… “Don’t listen to what your fellow citizens are saying about how we acted while we were with you. Listen instead to yourselves…”… his concern is ultimately not for himself but for his readers: it is “because of you”… that he demonstrated a blameless conduct."
**Claim:** Weima frames 1:5b as first of many firsthand-knowledge appeals used as persuasion against outside character attacks; blameless ethos is for the converts’ sake, not self-promotion alone.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C33 — Imitators of Paul and the Lord: affliction + Spirit-joy; not mere inward angst
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:6 (~slice ll. 348–400)
**Quote:** "…“you on your part became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in much affliction with joy that comes from the Holy Spirit”… it seems more likely… that Paul is thinking specifically of the opposition that he endured during his original preaching ministry in Thessalonica (2:2)… Malherbe argues that this “affliction”… [is] inward anxieties… But while the Thessalonian Christians did experience significant social dislocation… it would be clearly wrong to limit the suffering to inward anxieties… Therefore, the “affliction”… involves outward trials… more likely entailed severe social harassment and ostracism… “with joy that comes from the Holy Spirit”… their joy originates from the Holy Spirit, who enables them to see beyond their present suffering to their future deliverance."
**Claim:** Weima: indicative imitation (praise, with implicit ongoing challenge) of Paul-and-Lord centers on receiving the word under θλῖψις many; rejects Castelli-style pure power-abuse reading of imitation and Malherbe’s reduction to conversion anxiety; affliction = external hostility (social/economic/political ostracism, not primarily martyrdom); joy is Spirit-gifted eschatological perspective (cf. 1:10).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C34 — Thessalonians as τύπος to Macedonia and Achaia
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:7 + foreshadow note (~slice ll. 401–408)
**Quote:** "The word “example” (typos) properly refers to a mold… Figuratively… a model or pattern for ethical conduct… the Thessalonians who are not just an example for others to follow but indeed a kind of “mold” from which the lives of other believers are cast… he nowhere else states that a particular church has served as an inspiring example for believers in other locations… As 1:5 anticipates… defense… (2:1–16), so 1:6–7 looks ahead to… explaining Paul’s failure… to return… and of strengthening the believers… experiencing persecution (2:17–3:10)."
**Claim:** Weima stresses unique corporate praise: whole church as singular τύπος for Greece’s provinces; praise does pastoral/exhortative work and foreshadows persecution/absence material of 2:17–3:10 (also joy → 2:19–20; 3:9; imitation/receiving word → 2:13–16).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C35 — “Word of the Lord” echoed forth: verbal + nonverbal evangelism
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:8 (~slice ll. 411–428)
**Quote:** "…Paul has combined into one sentence two related yet distinct evangelistic activities… a proclaimed message (“the word of the Lord”) and an exemplary conversion (“your faith toward God”)… “of the Lord”… subjectively (“the word that comes from the Lord”)… “the Lord” refers… to Jesus Christ… The image… is that of a sound—the gospel message—emanating from the Thessalonian Christians and continuing to echo on and on… “not only in Macedonia and Achaia but in every place”… involves the use of hyperbole… On the other hand, the far-reaching impact… should not be overlooked… The expression “We have no need” in 1:8 constitutes an example of paraleipsis…"
**Claim:** Weima explains 1:8’s grammatical awkwardness as fusion of verbal proclamation (λόγος τοῦ κυρίου from the Lord Jesus, perfect “echoed forth”) and conversion-as-witness (“faith toward God”); geographic hyperbole with real travel-network plausibility; “no need to say anything” is rhetorical paraleipsis, not a hard claim contradicted by later boasting (2 Thess 1:4; 2 Cor 8).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C36 — εἴσοδος = “visit,” not “reception”: sincerity of mission-founding
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:9a (~slice ll. 432–436)
**Quote:** "A number of leading translations wrongly render this word as “reception” or “welcome”… The word, however, means “entrance” or “visit”… and clearly refers to the activities of Paul along with his fellow missionaries… stressing either the effectiveness or, more likely, the sincerity of Paul’s mission-founding visit (see the discussion of κενή in 2:1)… people throughout Macedonia, Achaia, and even beyond recognized that Paul’s mission-founding visit to Thessalonica exhibited none of these vain and dishonest practices."
**Claim:** Weima corrects NIV/NRSV-type “welcome” readings of εἴσοδος: the widespread report concerns the missionaries’ sincere entrance (hapax pair with 2:1), contrasted with self-serving traveling orators—another apologetic foreshadow of ch. 2.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C37 — “Turned to God from idols”: radical social break, not simple piety
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:9b (~slice ll. 440–441)
**Quote:** "Yet, in a society where cultic and social activities were intimately connected, there was nothing simple about turning to God from idols… Such action by Christians evoked feelings of resentment and anger… even led to charges that they were “atheists” (Barclay 1993: 514–15). Citizens of Thessalonica worried whether the gods, whose home on Mount Olympus they could see a mere fifty miles away… might punish the whole city… Turning from idols also meant a rejection of the imperial cult, thereby potentially jeopardizing Thessalonica’s favored status with Rome… a break that naturally incurred the resentment and anger of their fellow citizens (2:14)."
**Claim:** Weima (with Barclay) frames conversion as total renunciation of pagan cultic-social life—including imperial cult—explaining civic hostility and “atheist” charges; Olympus geography used illustratively for local religious imagination.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C38 — Two goals of conversion: serve living/true God; wait for Son
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:9c–10a (~slice ll. 442–448)
**Quote:** "This radical break or conversion involved change… with two specific goals… a present holiness (“in order to serve a living and true God”) and a future hope (“and to wait for his Son from the heavens”)… The verb δουλεύω… means not merely “to serve” but “to serve as a slave.”… In the OT (LXX)… total commitment to God… In this way, the first goal of conversion foreshadows the concern for holiness and proper moral conduct… (4:1–12 and 5:12–22)… “living” and “true”… highlight the contrast between the God of the Christian faith and the idols… here we have the first explicit reference to the second coming, or parousia, of Christ… the Thessalonians’ passion for serving God… is matched by their fervent hope in the future return…"
**Claim:** Weima: purpose infinitives balance ethics and eschatology—δουλεύειν as wholehearted OT-style slave-service of the living/true God (vs dead false idols; LXX background) vs ongoing waiting for the Son’s return; dual goal previews moral parenesis and parousia sections.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C39 — Jesus as Son raised from dead, rescuer from coming wrath
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:10 (~slice ll. 449–462)
**Quote:** "The description of the returning one as God’s “Son” is a bit unexpected… Paul uses the title “Son” to emphasize the intimate association between the one whose coming they await and the God to whom they have turned… This sonship… means that Jesus will be able to return and rescue them from the coming wrath… The mention of the resurrection here provides further support for the future hope… skillfully anticipates… 4:13–18, where the apostle grounds his words of comfort by first appealing to Jesus’s resurrection (4:14)… “the one who rescues us from the coming wrath.”… Paul’s use of the noun “wrath”… reveals that the source of this wrath is God… This third additional phrase foreshadows… 5:9… Today many stumble over the notion of an angry God… At odds with this conclusion… are the opening chapters of Romans… God’s wrath must be seen in the light of his justice… a necessary and just response to human sin."
**Claim:** Weima treats three appositions to “Son”: (1) God-raised (formulaic; anticipates 4:14 argument), (2) personal name “Jesus” (transition/Savior sense toward rescue), (3) present participle rescuer from coming divine wrath (anticipates 5:9). Rejects impersonal-wrath theories (contra Dodd); wrath is personal divine justice, already present yet awaiting completion; plural “heavens” not over-read as multi-tier cosmology.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C40 — Excursus 1: 1:9b–10 is Pauline, not pre-Pauline tradition
**Locus:** Excursus 1 (~slice ll. 492–525)
**Quote:** "The view that 1:9b–10 is pre-Pauline has become almost axiomatic in NT scholarship… “Here [1:9b–10] we have the mission-preaching to pagans in a nutshell” (Harnack)… Despite the seemingly compelling nature of such arguments, a number of factors suggest that 1:9b–10 comes from the hand of Paul (see Wanamaker 1990: 84–88; Hooker 1996; Furnish 2007: 48–49)… the material in 1:9b–10 is not really a summary of missionary preaching at all. Instead of describing the contents of the gospel, these verses recount the consequences that the gospel has had in the lives of the Thessalonians… These two verses summarize not traditional missionary preaching to Gentiles but what Paul is going to say in the body of the letter… Therefore 1 Thess. 1:9b–10 ought to be viewed not as pre-Pauline but, along with the rest of the thanksgiving section, as originating from the hand of the apostle."
**Claim:** Weima surveys and rejects majority pre-Pauline views (mission-kerygma to pagans; creed/baptismal hymn). Vocabulary “anomalies” (ἐπιστρέφω, δουλεύειν θεῷ, ἀληθινός, ἀναμένω, υἱός for parousia, plural οὐρανοί, article with νεκρῶν, ῥύομαι vs σῴζω) are overstated via Pauline parallels (esp. Gal 4:9; Rom 5:9–10; 7:24; 11:26). Missing cross/justification would be odd in a gospel summary—but 1:9b–10 narrates conversion **consequences**, not kerygma contents. Positive proposal: with 1:9a, the unit is a foreshadowing digest of body themes (visit/defense; turn-serve/holiness; wait/raise/rescue/eschatology).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C41 — Text-critical notes on 1:2–10 (selected)
**Locus:** Additional Notes 1:2–1:10 (~slice ll. 466–485)
**Quote:** "1:9. The apparent awkwardness of the shift (“report concerning us…”) led some scribes to “correct” the text to the smoother reading ὑμῶν (concerning you…)… Yet ἡμῶν (concerning us) not only has stronger MS support but also is the more difficult (and thus preferred) reading… 1:10. Wallace (1990) argues that the preposition ἐκ… is an early corruption of ἀπό… and that “there might be some support here for a pretribulational rapture” (478). Not only is the former reading (ἐκ) far superior on textual grounds, but Wallace’s theological inference from the latter reading (ἀπό) must also be judged to be a good example of eisegesis."
**Claim:** Weima’s text decisions include: ὑμῶν after “making mention” is later clarification; “our gospel” preferred over “God’s gospel” expansions; omit ἐν before πληροφορίᾳ; lean toward ἐν ὑμῖν at 1:5b as among-you conduct foreshadowing 2:1–16; reject “joy **and** the Holy Spirit”; singular τύπον collective; shorter “Macedonia and Achaia” in 1:8; ἡμῶν not ὑμῶν in 1:9a; ἐκ not ἀπό at 1:10 (anti-Wallace pretrib eisegesis).
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `parousia-1-thess-4`

### C42 — Pattern of alternating visit/response in chs. 1–2
**Locus:** Exegesis 1:6 transition; 1:9 shift (~slice ll. 350–367, 432–434)
**Quote:** "This shift is the first of three similar movements in the opening chapters of the letter: Paul’s mission-founding visit | The response of the Thessalonians … 1:5 | 1:6–8; 1:9a | 1:9b–10; 2:1–12 | 2:13–16… The apostle’s desire to defend himself accounts for the repeated shift in focus from himself along with his coworkers and their mission-founding visit to Thessalonica, to discuss the Thessalonian believers’ response to that visit…"
**Claim:** Weima identifies a rhetorical pattern—mission visit then convert response—repeated thrice (1:5→6–8; 1:9a→9b–10; 2:1–12→13–16), driven by apologetic concern for the founding ministry.
**Target pages:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`
